claims.claim: Posterior progenitors continue to be generated beyond the major period of anterior tuberal specification.
claims.source: Our work suggests that posterior progenitors continue to be generated beyond the major period of anterior tuberal specification, and scRNA-Seq profiling reveals that over time, the transcriptional profile of posterior tuberal progenitors changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo experiments and scRNA-Seq analysis showing continued presence of posterior markers at later stages.

claims.claim: Over time, the transcriptional profile of posterior tuberal progenitors changes.
claims.source: Our work suggests that posterior progenitors continue to be generated beyond the major period of anterior tuberal specification, and scRNA-Seq profiling reveals that over time, the transcriptional profile of posterior tuberal progenitors changes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis showing differential gene expression in FGF10+ cells over time.

claims.claim: There is a gradual upregulation of candidate molecular regulators of a gliogenic programme that likely initiates the transformation of posterior tuberal progenitors to the stem-like radial glial cells that characterise the late-embryonic tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.source: We describe a gradual upregulation of candidate molecular regulators of a gliogenic programme that likely initiates the transformation of posterior tuberal progenitors to the stem-like radial glial cells that characterise the late-embryonic tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq data showing upregulation of SOX8/9, ID genes, VIM, and FABP7 in later-stage progenitors, combined with inference about their role in gliogenesis.

claims.claim: SIX6 is barely detected at HH8.
claims.source: The tuberal marker, SIX6, is barely detected at HH8 (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and instead, HypFP cells, defined through FOXA2(low)/NKX2-1/SHH expression (Kim et al., 2022) extend to almost the tip of the neuraxis at this stage (Figure 1A and F; white arrows).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: HypFP cells extend to almost the tip of the neuraxis at HH8.
claims.source: The tuberal marker, SIX6, is barely detected at HH8 (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and instead, HypFP cells, defined through FOXA2(low)/NKX2-1/SHH expression (Kim et al., 2022) extend to almost the tip of the neuraxis at this stage (Figure 1A and F; white arrows).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and F, and is also supported by citation to previous work defining HypFP cells.

claims.claim: By HH10, SIX6 is detected within anterior-most hypothalamic floor plate-like cells (aHypFP cells), in a flat portion of anterior ventral neuroepithelium.
claims.source: By HH10, SIX6 is detected within anterior-most hypothalamic floor plate-like cells (aHypFP cells), in a flat portion of anterior ventral neuroepithelium (Figure 1B, G, H, I, yellow arrows) that lies between FOXG1+ve telencephalic cells and a characteristic flexure composed of more posterior HypFP cells (Figure 1B, H, I, blue arrows).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B, G, H, I.

claims.claim: Over HH10-HH20, the SIX6 domain lengthens and SIX6 becomes graded, high expression marking the anterior tuberal domain and weak/no expression in the posterior tuberal domain that overlies Rathke's pouch.
claims.source: Over HH10-HH20, the SIX6 domain lengthens and SIX6 becomes graded, high expression marking the anterior tuberal domain and weak/no expression in the posterior tuberal domain that overlies Rathke's pouch (Figure 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claims.claim: TBX2 and SIX6 are first detected between HH8–HH9, and show almost identical expression in aHypFP cells.
claims.source: TBX2 and SIX6 are first detected between HH8–HH9, and, surprisingly, show almost identical expression in aHypFP cells (Figure 1J, K, O and P; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E″).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1J, K, O, P and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E″.

claims.claim: After HH8-9, SIX6 and TBX2 gradually resolve to mark distinct anterior and posterior domains.
claims.source: Thereafter, SIX6 and TBX2 gradually resolve to mark distinct anterior and posterior domains (Figure 1L–N, Q and R; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1L-N, Q, R and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-I.

claims.claim: By HH13, the SIX6+ve domain has expanded considerably, and is composed of SIX6+ve and SIX6/SHH+ve cells.
claims.source: By HH13, the SIX6+ve domain has expanded considerably, and is composed of SIX6+ve and SIX6/SHH+ve cells, while SHH starts to be downregulated in TBX2+ve posterior cells (Figure 1N and R).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1N and R.

claims.claim: SHH starts to be downregulated in TBX2+ve posterior cells by HH13.
claims.source: By HH13, the SIX6+ve domain has expanded considerably, and is composed of SIX6+ve and SIX6/SHH+ve cells, while SHH starts to be downregulated in TBX2+ve posterior cells (Figure 1N and R).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1N and R.

claims.claim: By HH17, the SIX6/SHH domain is neurogenic (ASCL1+ve).
claims.source: By HH17, the SIX6/SHH domain is neurogenic (ASCL1+ve), and anterior SIX6+ve cells are more differentiated, expressing the neuronal precursor cell marker, ISL1 (Figure 1T–T″).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1T-T″.

claims.claim: By HH17, anterior SIX6+ve cells are more differentiated, expressing the neuronal precursor cell marker, ISL1.
claims.source: By HH17, the SIX6/SHH domain is neurogenic (ASCL1+ve), and anterior SIX6+ve cells are more differentiated, expressing the neuronal precursor cell marker, ISL1 (Figure 1T–T″).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1T-T″.

claims.claim: pSMAD1/5/8 is detected immediately after HH8 in aHypFP cells.
claims.source: pSMAD1/5/8 is detected immediately after HH8 in aHypFP cells (Figure 2A–B′′′; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2A-B′′′ and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: From HH8 until at least HH17, pSMAD1/5/8 is always detected in aHypFP cells and cells just anterior to these.
claims.source: Thereafter, and at least until HH17 (the latest stage analysed) pSMAD1/5/8 is always detected in aHypFP cells and cells just anterior to these (Figure 2C–C′′′; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2C-C′′′ and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells overlie Rathke's pouch and/or its LHX3+ve surface ectoderm precursors.
claims.source: Analysis of pSMAD1/5/8 in combination with a range of markers shows that pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells overlie Rathke's pouch and/or its LHX3+ve surface ectoderm precursors (Figure 2D–F, yellow dashed line), are distinct from FOXG1+ve telencephalic progenitors, are posterior to ASCL1+ve anterior tuberal neurogenic cells markers, and overlap with, but extend posterior to TBX2+ve cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claims.claim: pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells are distinct from FOXG1+ve telencephalic progenitors.
claims.source: Analysis of pSMAD1/5/8 in combination with a range of markers shows that pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells overlie Rathke's pouch and/or its LHX3+ve surface ectoderm precursors (Figure 2D–F, yellow dashed line), are distinct from FOXG1+ve telencephalic progenitors, are posterior to ASCL1+ve anterior tuberal neurogenic cells markers, and overlap with, but extend posterior to TBX2+ve cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells are posterior to ASCL1+ve anterior tuberal neurogenic cells.
claims.source: Analysis of pSMAD1/5/8 in combination with a range of markers shows that pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells overlie Rathke's pouch and/or its LHX3+ve surface ectoderm precursors (Figure 2D–F, yellow dashed line), are distinct from FOXG1+ve telencephalic progenitors, are posterior to ASCL1+ve anterior tuberal neurogenic cells markers, and overlap with, but extend posterior to TBX2+ve cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells overlap with, but extend posterior to TBX2+ve cells.
claims.source: Analysis of pSMAD1/5/8 in combination with a range of markers shows that pSMAD1/5/8+ve cells overlie Rathke's pouch and/or its LHX3+ve surface ectoderm precursors (Figure 2D–F, yellow dashed line), are distinct from FOXG1+ve telencephalic progenitors, are posterior to ASCL1+ve anterior tuberal neurogenic cells markers, and overlap with, but extend posterior to TBX2+ve cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: At all times, pSMAD1/5/8 straddles aHypFP cells and posterior-most cells of the lengthening tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.source: In summary, pSMAD1/5/8 is first detected just after HH8, and at all times thereafter straddles aHypFP cells and posterior-most cells of the lengthening tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.evidence: This claim is a summary statement supported by the immunolabeling data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Cells within the pSMAD1/5/8+ve aHypFP region at HH10 gave rise to SHH+ve anterior progenitors at HH17.
claims.source: Further processing by HCR in situ hybridisation showed that cells within the pSMAD1/5/8+ve aHypFP region at HH10 gave rise to SHH +ve anterior progenitors at HH17 (Figure 2K and K′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fate-mapping experiments shown in Figure 2K and K′.

claims.claim: Cells within the aHypFP region at HH10 gave rise to regions located anterior to TBX2+ve progenitors at HH17.
claims.source: Additional analyses showed that cells within the aHypFP region at HH10 gave rise to regions located anterior to TBX2+ve progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fate-mapping experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E, F.

claims.claim: Anterior neurogenic progenitors are derived from progenitors that transiently activate BMP Smads.
claims.source: This implies that anterior neurogenic progenitors are derived from progenitors that transiently activate BMP signalling, and that pSMAD1/5/8 does not mark a stable (label-retaining) population.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the fate-mapping data showing that cells in the pSMAD1/5/8+ zone at HH10 give rise to anterior progenitors at HH17.

claims.claim: pSMAD1/5/8 does not mark a stable (label-retaining) population.
claims.source: This implies that anterior neurogenic progenitors are derived from progenitors that transiently activate BMP signalling, and that pSMAD1/5/8 does not mark a stable (label-retaining) population.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the fate-mapping data showing that cells in the pSMAD1/5/8+ zone at HH10 give rise to anterior progenitors at HH17, rather than remaining in the posterior zone.

claims.claim: More posterior HypFP cells at HH10 that are pSMAD1/5/8 negative give rise to posterior tuberal progenitors at HH17.
claims.source: To confirm this, we targeted more posterior HypFP cells (Figure 2L, N, pink arrow; Figure 2—figure supplement 2G) that are pSMAD1/5/8 negative at HH10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). We found that these give rise to posterior tuberal progenitors at HH17 (SIX6/SHH-ve, FGF10+ve) (Figure 2M, O, P, P′, pink arrow; Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), sometimes even contributing to (posterior-most) anterior tuberal progenitors (SIX6/SHH+ve, FGF10-ve) (Figure 2M, O, P and P′; Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fate-mapping experiments shown in Figure 2L-P and Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-H.

claims.claim: Cells that lie even more posteriorly at HH10 fate-mapped to the diencephalic floor plate.
claims.source: Cells that lie even more posteriorly at HH10 fate-mapped to the diencephalic floor plate (Figure 2L and M, blue arrow).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fate-mapping experiments shown in Figure 2L and M.

claims.claim: Cells maintain their relative antero-posterior spatial positions within the neuroectoderm between HH10 and HH17, with no evidence of mixing.
claims.source: Double- or triple-label analyses with DiI and DiO, further, suggested that cells maintain their relative antero-posterior spatial positions within the neuroectoderm between HH10 and HH17, with no evidence of mixing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I–N), an idea supported through time-lapse imaging of DiI/DiO-targeted isolated neural tubes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2O–R).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by double/triple-label fate-mapping experiments and time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2I-R.

claims.claim: The tuberal hypothalamus is generated through a conveyor-belt mechanism, through a programme that is initiated when canonical BMP signalling is activated in aHypFP cells, and then relayed back through more posterior HypFP cells.
claims.source: These results suggest that the tuberal hypothalamus is generated through a conveyor-belt mechanism, through a programme that is initiated when canonical BMP signalling is activated in aHypFP cells, and then relayed back through more posterior HypFP cells (schematised in Figure 2Q).
claims.evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the fate-mapping and pSMAD1/5/8 expression data.

claims.claim: The appearance of pSMAD1/5/8+ve nuclei is associated with the upregulation of tuberal progenitor markers and the loss of FOXA2.
claims.source: The appearance of pSMAD1/5/8+ve nuclei is associated with the upregulation of tuberal progenitor markers and the loss of FOXA2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial and temporal analysis of marker expression shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: As tuberal cells are generated, the zone of active BMP signalling, and underlying tissues, move relatively posteriorly.
claims.source: As tuberal cells are generated, the zone of active BMP signalling, and underlying tissues, move relatively posteriorly.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that pSMAD1/5/8 is consistently found at the posterior edge of the tuberal domain, and fate-mapping showing relative posterior displacement of underlying tissues.

claims.claim: Newly specified posterior tuberal markers remain closely associated with the pSMAD1/5/8+ve zone, while the anterior tuberal domain expands.
claims.source: Newly specified posterior tuberal markers remain closely associated with the pSMAD1/5/8+ve zone, while the anterior tuberal domain expands.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of marker expression showing TBX2 and FGF10 expression overlapping with pSMAD1/5/8, while SIX6/SHH domain expands anteriorly.

claims.claim: Tuberal progenitor cells are generated sequentially, with prospective anterior tuberal cells moving through the BMP signalling zone earlier than prospective posterior tuberal cells.
claims.source: We conclude that tuberal progenitor cells are generated sequentially, with prospective anterior tuberal cells moving through the BMP signalling zone earlier than prospective posterior tuberal cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on the fate-mapping and marker expression data.

claims.claim: From HH9 to HH17, LHX3+ve ectoderm/Rathke's pouch tip cells express BMP2 and BMP7.
claims.source: From HH9 to HH17, LHX3+ve ectoderm/Rathke's pouch tip cells express BMP2 and BMP7 (Figure 3A–F, blue arrows).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A-F.

claims.claim: BMP2 and BMP7 are also expressed in hypothalamic cells.
claims.source: However, BMP2 and BMP7 are also expressed in hypothalamic cells (Figure 3A–F, pink arrows; Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A-F and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: TBX2 is first upregulated in cells that express high levels of BMP2 and lie just anterior to BMP7+ve cells.
claims.source: Indeed, HCR analysis shows that TBX2 is first upregulated in cells that express high levels of BMP2 and lie just anterior to BMP7+ve cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: From HH10 onwards, hypothalamic neuroepithelium-intrinsic factors are sufficient to maintain tuberal hypothalamic regionalisation and neurogenesis.
claims.source: We conclude that, although BMP ligands from non-hypothalamic structures are required to initiate tuberal development (Dale et al., 1997; Dale et al., 1999), from HH10 onwards, hypothalamic neuroepithelium-intrinsic factors are sufficient to maintain tuberal hypothalamic regionalisation and neurogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments showing that isolated hypothalamic tissue can develop tuberal markers and organization in the absence of surrounding tissues, combined with citations to previous work on early induction.

claims.claim: BMP ligands from non-hypothalamic structures are required to initiate tuberal development.
claims.source: We conclude that, although BMP ligands from non-hypothalamic structures are required to initiate tuberal development (Dale et al., 1997; Dale et al., 1999), from HH10 onwards, hypothalamic neuroepithelium-intrinsic factors are sufficient to maintain tuberal hypothalamic regionalisation and neurogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Isolated HH10 hypothalamic explants cultured to HH13 equivalent generate domains that show the same organisation as in vivo.
claims.source: Similar explants cultured to a HH13 equivalent grew and generated domains that showed the same organisation as in vivo. SHH and FGF10 now resolved into overlapping domains (Figure 3L–L″), and distinct but overlapping regions expressing SIX6, SIX6/SHH and TBX2 were detected, as in vivo (compare Figure 3M–M″ to Figure 1N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 3L-M″.

claims.claim: After culture to an HH24 equivalent, isolated HH10 hypothalamic explants show discrete but overlapping domains of ISL1/SHH, pSMAD1/5/8, and EMX2 expression.
claims.source: After culture to an HH24 equivalent, explants had grown extensively and showed discrete but overlapping domains of marker expression: an ISL1/SHH+ve domain, adjacent to a pSMAD1/5/8+ve domain, and then an EMX2+ve domain (Figure 3N–N″″).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 3N-N″″.

claims.claim: Isolated HH10 hypothalamic explants cultured to HH24 equivalent generate a spatial pattern similar to that in vivo, composed of ISL1/SHH+ve anterior neurogenic cells, then pSMAD1/5/8+ve tuberal progenitor cells, then EMX2+ve mammillary cells.
claims.source: This pattern suggests that isolated explants, free from any possible influence of surrounding tissues, have grown to generate a spatial pattern that is similar to that in vivo, that is, composed of ISL1/SHH+ve anterior neurogenic cells, then pSMAD1/5/8+ve tuberal progenitor cells, then EMX2+ve mammillary cells (Figure 3O–Q).
claims.evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the ex vivo culture data, comparing explant marker expression to in vivo patterns shown in Figure 3O-Q.

claims.claim: Exposure of HH6-HH8 HypFP cells to BMPs leads to the generation of tuberal cells.
claims.source: Our findings predict that exposure of HypFP cells to BMPs will lead to the generation of tuberal cells.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings, which is then tested in the subsequent experiments.

claims.claim: HH6-HH8 anterior explants cultured to HH14 equivalent express tuberal progenitor markers (SIX6/NKX2-1/SHH/TBX2) and anterior-tuberal neuronal markers (NR5A1, POMC).
claims.source: After culture to a ~HH14 equivalent, anterior explants expressed tuberal progenitor markers (SIX6/NKX2-1/SHH/TBX2), and anterior-tuberal neuronal markers (NR5A1, POMC) (Figure 4, row B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 4, row B.

claims.claim: HH6-HH8 posterior explants cultured to HH14 equivalent do not express tuberal markers, but instead express SHH/FOXA2 markers that define the later floor plate and supramammillary hypothalamus.
claims.source: By contrast, posterior explants did not express tuberal markers, but instead, expressed SHH/FOXA2 (Figure 4, rows C, E) markers that define the later floor plate and supramammillary hypothalamus (Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 4, rows C and E, and citation to previous work defining these markers.

claims.claim: HH6-HH8 posterior explants exposed to 32 nM BMP2/7 upregulate tuberal markers, including TBX2, SIX6, NR5A1 and POMC.
claims.source: However, posterior explants that were exposed to 32 nM BMP2/7 upregulated tuberal markers, including TBX2, SIX6, NR5A1 and POMC (Figure 4F–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments with BMP2/7 treatment shown in Figure 4F-H.

claims.claim: BMP2/7 can induce HypFP cells to form tuberal cells.
claims.source: We conclude that BMP2/7 can induce HypFP cells to form tuberal cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ex vivo experiments showing that BMP2/7 treatment of posterior explants induces tuberal marker expression.

claims.claim: Implantation of Noggin-soaked beads in the tuberal region of HH9-HH10 embryos results in partial suppression of tuberal development at HH18.
claims.source: Implantation of beads, soaked with the BMP inhibitor Noggin (Smith and Harland, 1992) in the tuberal region of an HH9–HH10 embryo (Figure 5A) resulted in partial suppression of tuberal development at HH18. The SIX6+ve anterior domain was significantly reduced, there was no/little sign of the TBX2+ve posterior domain, and SHH was abnormally maintained in the region where TBX2 is normally expressed (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Noggin bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: Noggin exposure results in a significantly reduced SIX6+ve anterior domain.
claims.source: Implantation of beads, soaked with the BMP inhibitor Noggin (Smith and Harland, 1992) in the tuberal region of an HH9–HH10 embryo (Figure 5A) resulted in partial suppression of tuberal development at HH18. The SIX6+ve anterior domain was significantly reduced, there was no/little sign of the TBX2+ve posterior domain, and SHH was abnormally maintained in the region where TBX2 is normally expressed (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Noggin bead implantation experiments and quantification shown in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: Noggin exposure results in no/little sign of the TBX2+ve posterior domain.
claims.source: Implantation of beads, soaked with the BMP inhibitor Noggin (Smith and Harland, 1992) in the tuberal region of an HH9–HH10 embryo (Figure 5A) resulted in partial suppression of tuberal development at HH18. The SIX6+ve anterior domain was significantly reduced, there was no/little sign of the TBX2+ve posterior domain, and SHH was abnormally maintained in the region where TBX2 is normally expressed (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Noggin bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: Noggin exposure results in SHH being abnormally maintained in the region where TBX2 is normally expressed.
claims.source: Implantation of beads, soaked with the BMP inhibitor Noggin (Smith and Harland, 1992) in the tuberal region of an HH9–HH10 embryo (Figure 5A) resulted in partial suppression of tuberal development at HH18. The SIX6+ve anterior domain was significantly reduced, there was no/little sign of the TBX2+ve posterior domain, and SHH was abnormally maintained in the region where TBX2 is normally expressed (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo Noggin bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: Noggin-exposed embryos show that pSMAD1/5/8 is downregulated only transiently.
claims.source: Indeed, examination of Noggin-exposed embryos showed that pSMAD1/5/8 is downregulated only transiently (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: HH6-8 anterior explants cultured to HH18 equivalent robustly express the tuberal markers TBX2/SIX6, and do not express the supramammillary/floor plate marker, FOXA2.
claims.source: We first confirmed that anterior explants cultured to an HH18 equivalent robustly express the tuberal markers TBX2/SIX6, and do not express the supramammillary/floor plate marker, FOXA2 (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Many HH6-8 anterior explants cultured to HH18 equivalent express the anterior neuronal precursor marker, ISL1.
claims.source: Further, we showed that many express the anterior neuronal precursor marker, ISL1 (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: HH6-8 anterior explants cultured from the outset in 300 ng/μl Noggin show little or no expression of SIX6, TBX2 or ISL1, but instead robustly express FOXA2.
claims.source: In contrast, anterior explants cultured from the outset in 300 ng/μl Noggin showed little or no expression of either SIX6, TBX2 or ISL1, but instead, robustly expressed FOXA2 (Figure 5G and H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments with Noggin treatment shown in Figure 5G and H.

claims.claim: When HH6-8 anterior explants are cultured in control medium to HH10, both SIX6 and TBX2 are detected.
claims.source: When anterior explants were cultured in control medium to the equivalent of HH10, both SIX6 and TBX2 were detected (Figure 5E, insets).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 5E, insets.

claims.claim: If HH6-8 anterior explants are cultured in control medium to HH10, and then cultured with Noggin to HH18, SIX6 and ISL1 are more robustly detected, but little/no TBX2 is detected.
claims.source: However, if anterior explants were cultured in control medium to HH10, and then cultured with Noggin to HH18, SIX6 and ISL1 were now more robustly detected, but little/no TBX2 was detected (Figure 5I and J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments with delayed Noggin treatment shown in Figure 5I and J.

claims.claim: Anterior specification is well underway by HH10.
claims.source: This suggests that TBX2+ve cells generated by HH10 have progressed to anterior cells, and that anterior specification is well underway by HH10, but that a longer or later period of BMP exposure is required for the de novo generation of posterior progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ex vivo experiments showing that Noggin treatment after HH10 promotes anterior marker expression.

claims.claim: A longer or later period of BMP exposure is required for the de novo generation of posterior progenitors.
claims.source: This suggests that TBX2+ve cells generated by HH10 have progressed to anterior cells, and that anterior specification is well underway by HH10, but that a longer or later period of BMP exposure is required for the de novo generation of posterior progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ex vivo experiments showing that Noggin treatment after HH10 still affects TBX2 expression.

claims.claim: The addition of Noggin to HH6-8 anterior explants at 48 hr (equivalent of ~HH14) had little effect, with FOXA2, TBX2, SIX6 and ISL1 detected similarly to controls.
claims.source: The addition of Noggin to anterior explants at 48 hr, which is the equivalent of ~HH14, had little effect, with FOXA2, TBX2, SIX6 and ISL1 detected similarly to the frequency and levels observed in controls (Figure 5H–H″″).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments with delayed Noggin treatment shown in Figure 5K and L.

claims.claim: De novo specification of posterior progenitors has occurred by HH14.
claims.source: This indicates that de novo specification of posterior progenitors has occurred by HH14.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ex vivo experiments showing that Noggin treatment after HH14 has little effect on marker expression.

claims.claim: Ectopic BMPs reduce or eliminate SIX6/SHH+ve anterior tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: Ectopic BMPs reduced, or eliminated, SIX6/SHH +ve anterior tuberal progenitors (white brackets in Figure 6A–C″′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 6A-C″′.

claims.claim: The distancing of tuberal progenitors from the source of BMP in the posterior hypothalamus is a critical step in their specification to an anterior neurogenic state.
claims.source: This supports the idea that the distancing of tuberal progenitors from the source of BMP in the posterior hypothalamus that occurs in vivo is a critical step in their specification to an anterior neurogenic state.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the BMP bead implantation experiments showing that prolonged BMP exposure prevents anterior specification.

claims.claim: Ectopic BMPs result in a significant increase in intensity of TBX2.
claims.source: (E) Graph showing a significant increase in intensity of TBX2 following BMP2/7 bead implantation p < 0.05, unpaired t test; error bars show SEM; n = 3 embryos/condition.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of TBX2 expression after BMP2/7 bead implantation shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Ectopic BMPs alter the profile of the posterior tuberal domain, with cells showing a 'mixed profile' (SIX6/TBX2/SHH+ve), similar to that detected at HH9.
claims.source: At the same time, ectopic BMPs altered the profile of the posterior tuberal domain (pink brackets in Figure 6A″–C′). Cells showed a 'mixed profile' (SIX6/TBX2/SHH+ve), similar to that detected at HH9.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 6A-C′.

claims.claim: Ectopic BMPs result in marginally reduced SHH expression in the anterior lateral hypothalamus.
claims.source: Additionally, SHH expression was marginally reduced in the anterior lateral hypothalamus, while TBX2 expression was significantly increased (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Ectopic BMPs eliminate FST expression, which at HH13 is restricted to a domain located just dorsal to the anterior intrahypothalamic diagonal.
claims.source: No obvious changes in expression of the prethalamic marker PAX6 were detected, but FST, which at this stage is restricted to a domain located just dorsal to the anterior intrahypothalamic diagonal (ID) (Shimogori et al., 2010), was eliminated (Figure 6B and D, white arrows).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 6B and D, and citation to previous work defining FST expression.

claims.claim: Excess BMP signalling prevents developing tuberal progenitors from developing beyond an early 'mixed' state.
claims.source: These observations extend previous studies that demonstrate that BMP signalling induces TBX2 expression (Manning et al., 2006), but suggest additionally that excess BMP signalling prevents developing tuberal progenitors from developing beyond an early 'mixed' state.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that ectopic BMP exposure results in cells with a mixed marker profile similar to early stages, combined with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Exposure to BMP2/7 at HH10 either reduces (n=4) or eliminates (n=2) anterior tuberal progenitors at HH18, as measured through reduction or loss of SIX6 and SHH.
claims.source: Exposure to BMP2/7 either reduced (n = 4) or eliminated (n = 2) anterior tuberal progenitors, as measured through a reduction or loss of SIX6 and SHH (Figure 6F–G′ and K; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments analyzed at HH18, shown in Figure 6F-G′ and K, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-F′.

claims.claim: BMP-treated embryos examined at HH18 show a reduction or loss of posterior tuberal progenitors, reflected in decreased or absent expression of TBX2 and FGF10.
claims.source: Surprisingly, and in contrast to embryos examined at HH13, BMP-treated embryos also showed a reduction or loss of posterior tuberal progenitors, reflected in the decreased or absent expression of TBX2 and FGF10 (Figure 6H–I′; Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, G′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments analyzed at HH18, shown in Figure 6H-I′ and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, G′.

claims.claim: FOXA2 expression in the floor plate and supramammillary hypothalamus appears normal after BMP2/7 treatment.
claims.source: By contrast, FOXA2 expression in the floor plate and supramammillary hypothalamus appeared normal (Figure 6J and J′; Figure 6—figure supplement 1H, H′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments shown in Figure 6J and J′, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1H, H′.

claims.claim: BMP2/7 treatment results in reduction or loss of the anterior and posterior tuberal progenitor territories as well as the intrahypothalamic diagonal, as judged by reduction or loss of RAX, NKX2-1, NKX2-2 and FST expression.
claims.source: Additional rounds of multiplex HCR confirmed the reduction or loss of the anterior and posterior tuberal progenitor territories as well as the ID, as judged by reduction or loss of RAX, NKX2-1, NKX2-2 and FST expression (Figure 6L–O′ and Q; Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–J′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiplex HCR analysis of BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6L-O′ and Q, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-J′.

claims.claim: Posterior hypothalamic regions are barely affected by BMP2/7 treatment: expression of the supramammillary and mammillary markers PITX2 and EMX2 are maintained.
claims.source: These analyses confirmed that posterior hypothalamic regions were barely affected: expression of the supramammillary and mammillary markers PITX2 and EMX2 were maintained (Figure 6—figure supplement 1K–L′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiplex HCR analysis of BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1K-L′.

claims.claim: The telencephalic marker FOXG1 is unaffected by BMP2/7 treatment, maintaining its relation to the optic stalk opening.
claims.source: The telencephalic marker FOXG1, likewise, was unaffected, maintaining its relation to the optic stalk opening (Figure 6P and P′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiplex HCR analysis of BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6P and P′.

claims.claim: The reduction/loss of tuberal progenitor domains after BMP2/7 treatment is accompanied by marked changes in anterior ventral forebrain morphology: the optic stalk fails to narrow, resulting in a gaping entrance to the optic stalk and copious SIX6/RAX/PAX6+ve eye tissue within.
claims.source: The reduction/loss of tuberal progenitor domains was accompanied by marked changes in anterior ventral forebrain morphology: the optic stalk failed to narrow, resulting in a gaping entrance to the optic stalk and copious SIX6/RAX/PAX6+ive eye tissue within (Figure 6F, F′, L, L′, O, O′, R, R′ and W).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis and marker expression in BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6F, F′, L, L′, O, O′, R, R′ and W.

claims.claim: Excessive BMP exposure leads ultimately to a loss of expression of molecular markers of both anterior and posterior tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: We conclude that excessive BMP exposure leads ultimately to a loss of expression of molecular markers of both anterior and—unexpectedly—posterior tuberal progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments showing loss of both anterior and posterior tuberal markers.

claims.claim: ISL1 expression is absent or weaker/reduced after exposure to BMPs, in a manner that correlates with the loss or reduction of SIX6/SHH+ve anterior progenitors.
claims.source: ISL1 expression was absent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1M, M′), or weaker/reduced (Figure 6S, S′) after exposure to BMPs, in a manner that correlated with the loss or reduction of SIX6/SHH+ve anterior progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of ISL1 expression in BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6S, S′ and Figure 6—figure supplement 1M, M′.

claims.claim: In embryos with a partial loss of the tuberal hypothalamus after BMP treatment, expression of the Notch target gene HES5 is dramatically reduced.
claims.source: Further analysis showed that in embryos with a partial loss of the tuberal hypothalamus, expression of the Notch target gene HES5 was dramatically reduced (Figure 6T and T′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of HES5 expression in BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6T and T′.

claims.claim: Notch maintains the progenitor state in the chick hypothalamus.
claims.source: Notch maintains the progenitor state in the chick hypothalamus (Hamdi-Rozé et al., 2020; Place et al., 2022; Ratié et al., 2014, Ratié et al., 2013; Ware et al., 2016), so we asked whether the loss of HES5 expression was associated with ectopic neurogenesis, examining expression of the neurogenic progenitor marker DLL1, and the neural precursor marker ELAVL4.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Expression of the neurogenic progenitor marker DLL1 and the neural precursor marker ELAVL4 are not obviously different in the residual hypothalamic domain of BMP-treated embryos in comparison to controls.
claims.source: Neither, however, was obviously different in the residual hypothalamic domain of BMP-treated embryos in comparison to controls (Figure 6U–V′).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of DLL1 and ELAVL4 expression in BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6U-V′.

claims.claim: An increase in neurogenesis may be balanced out by the presence of fewer progenitor cells in BMP-treated embryos.
claims.source: A possible interpretation is that an increase in neurogenesis may be balanced out by the presence of fewer progenitor cells (Figure 6F–K and Q).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data, suggesting a possible explanation for the observation that neurogenic markers are present despite loss of progenitors.

claims.claim: BMP-treated embryos show a significant reduction in M-phase progenitors in the tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.source: Supporting this possibility, BMP-treated embryos showed a significant reduction in M-phase progenitors in the tuberal hypothalamus (Figure 6X–Z).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of pH3+ cells in BMP2/7-treated embryos shown in Figure 6X-Z.

claims.claim: Excessive BMP levels acutely inhibit anterior tuberal specification.
claims.source: We conclude that excessive BMP levels acutely inhibit anterior tuberal specification, and over time result in more widespread disruption, including the loss of posterior progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments showing acute effects on anterior markers and later effects on posterior markers.

claims.claim: Excessive BMP levels over time result in more widespread disruption, including the loss of posterior progenitors.
claims.source: We conclude that excessive BMP levels acutely inhibit anterior tuberal specification, and over time result in more widespread disruption, including the loss of posterior progenitors.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments showing time-dependent effects.

claims.claim: Throughout the period HH10-HH17, pSMAD1/5/8+ve nuclei lie within/overlap with cells that express FGF10.
claims.source: Throughout the period HH10-HH17, pSMAD1/5/8+ve nuclei lie within/overlap with cells that express FGF10 (Figure 7A; Figure 3O–Q), allowing us to use FGF10 expression as a proxy for cells expressing pSMAD1/5/8.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-expression analysis shown in Figure 7A and Figure 3O-Q.

claims.claim: FGF10+ve cells show differential expression of a number of known developmental regulators between early (more anterior) and late (more posterior) stages.
claims.source: This analysis showed differential expression of a number of known developmental regulators between early (more anterior) and late (more posterior) FGF10+ve cells (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: CHRD (Chordin), BMP2/7 and SST show enriched expression in early stage (HH8–HH10) tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: CHRD (Chordin), BMP2/7 and SST showed enriched expression in early stage (HH8–HH10) tuberal progenitors, whereas the retinoic acid binding protein CRABP1, WNT5A, and the growth factor CTGF showed enriched expression in later-stage tuberal progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: CRABP1, WNT5A, and CTGF show enriched expression in later-stage tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: CHRD (Chordin), BMP2/7 and SST showed enriched expression in early stage (HH8–HH10) tuberal progenitors, whereas the retinoic acid binding protein CRABP1, WNT5A, and the growth factor CTGF showed enriched expression in later-stage tuberal progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The WNT/FGF pathway inhibitor SHISA2 is expressed in early, but not late, tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: The WNT/FGF pathway inhibitor SHISA2 was expressed in early, but not late, tuberal progenitors, and expression of the canonical WNT mediator (and adherens junction component) CTNNB1 (β-catenin) increased over time.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Expression of CTNNB1 (β-catenin) increases over time in tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: The WNT/FGF pathway inhibitor SHISA2 was expressed in early, but not late, tuberal progenitors, and expression of the canonical WNT mediator (and adherens junction component) CTNNB1 (β-catenin) increased over time.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Changes in expression levels of LFNG, HES5 and HES5-like indicate a gradual increase in NOTCH signalling over time in tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: Changes in expression levels of the NOTCH signalling pathway modulator LFNG, and its target genes HES5 and HES5-like indicated a gradual increase in NOTCH signalling over time.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C, combined with inference about NOTCH signaling activity.

claims.claim: The transcription factors ONECUT1, ID1, ID2, ID4, SOX8 and SOX9 show enriched expression in later-stage FGF10+ve tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: Likewise, the transcription factors ONECUT1, ID1, ID2, ID4, SOX8 and SOX9 showed enriched expression in later-stage FGF10+ve tuberal progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: HCR analyses confirm the upregulation of ID2 and ID4 in later-stage (posterior) tuberal progenitors.
claims.source: HCR analyses confirm the upregulation of ID2 and ID4 in later-stage (posterior) tuberal progenitors (Figure 7D–I; Place et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HCR in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D-I and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Both abrupt (e.g., BMP2/7, SHISA2) and gradual changes in gene expression are detected in FGF10+ve cells, conferring a distinct transcriptional profile upon FGF10+ve cells at each stage sequenced.
claims.source: We conclude that both abrupt (e.g., BMP2/7, SHISA2) and gradual changes in gene expression are detected, conferring a distinct transcriptional profile upon FGF10+ve cells at each stage sequenced.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells over time.

claims.claim: Anterior and posterior tuberal progenitors are specified by HH14.
claims.source: Our ex vivo experiments suggested that anterior and posterior tuberal progenitors are specified by HH14 (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo experiments with Noggin treatment at different time points shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Noggin eliminates TBX2 and promotes continued expression of anterior markers in posterior tuberal progenitors isolated at HH15 and cultured to HH17.
claims.source: Additional ex vivo experiments, isolating posterior tuberal progenitors at HH15 and culturing them to HH17 show that Noggin eliminates TBX2 and promotes continued expression of anterior markers (Figure 7J–M).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments shown in Figure 7J-M.

claims.claim: BMPs actively repress the anterior tuberal program after HH15.
claims.source: Therefore, BMPs actively repress the anterior tuberal program after HH15, and this switch in competence coincides with the transcriptional onset of a large set of transcription factors (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ex vivo experiments showing that Noggin treatment after HH15 promotes anterior marker expression, combined with the scRNA-Seq data showing transcriptional changes.

claims.claim: The switch in competence of tuberal progenitors coincides with the transcriptional onset of a large set of transcription factors.
claims.source: Therefore, BMPs actively repress the anterior tuberal program after HH15, and this switch in competence coincides with the transcriptional onset of a large set of transcription factors (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis showing upregulation of transcription factors in later-stage progenitors.

claims.claim: Upregulation of SOX8/9 and ID family gene expression has been previously reported in late-stage neuronal progenitors in mammals.
claims.source: Upregulation of SOX8/9 and ID family gene expression has been previously reported in late-stage neuronal progenitors in mammals (Clark et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2021; Sagner et al., 2021; Telley et al., 2019), raising the possibility that the expression of these genes in later posterior tuberal progenitors is associated with neurogenesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature in mammals.

claims.claim: The upregulation of SOX8/9 and ID genes in later posterior tuberal progenitors may be directly linked to the transition of posterior tuberal progenitors from a neuroepithelial to radial glial-like state.
claims.source: Alternatively, this upregulation may be directly linked to the transition of posterior tuberal progenitors from a neuroepithelial to radial glial-like state, a process that is regulated by SOX9 in the developing spinal cord (Scott et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data, supported by citation to previous work on SOX9 in spinal cord development.

claims.claim: SOX9 regulates the transition from neuroepithelial to radial glial state in the developing spinal cord.
claims.source: Alternatively, this upregulation may be directly linked to the transition of posterior tuberal progenitors from a neuroepithelial to radial glial-like state, a process that is regulated by SOX9 in the developing spinal cord (Scott et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The radial glial markers VIM and FABP7 are upregulated in FGF10+ve progenitors at HH20/21.
claims.source: In support of this, the radial glial markers VIM and FABP7 are upregulated in FGF10+ve progenitors at HH20/21 (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The molecular changes in later posterior tuberal progenitors may reflect the onset of the transition of FGF10+ve posterior tuberal neuroepithelial progenitors to the FGF10+ve radial glial-like tanycytes that characterise the late-embryonic and adult tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.source: These molecular changes, therefore, may reflect the onset of the transition of FGF10+ve posterior tuberal neuroepithelial progenitors to the FGF10+ve radial glial-like tanycytes that characterise the late-embryonic and adult tuberal hypothalamus (Goodman et al., 2020; Haan et al., 2013; Robins et al., 2013; Yoo et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the molecular data, supported by citations to previous work on tanycytes.

claims.claim: In many regions of the CNS, including the cortex and retina, waves of neuronal precursors are generated and laid down in a topological sequence as stem-like/progenitor cells undergo temporal switches in developmental potential.
claims.source: In many regions of the CNS, including the cortex and retina, waves of neuronal precursors are generated and laid down in a topological sequence as stem-like/progenitor cells undergo temporal switches in developmental potential (Heavner and Pevny, 2012; Kawaguchi, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on cortex and retina development.

claims.claim: In the tuberal hypothalamus, spatial pattern emerges through a series of transient progenitors, as a wave of BMP signalling sweeps from anterior to posterior through HypFP cells.
claims.source: Our studies show, by contrast, that in the tuberal hypothalamus, spatial pattern emerges through a series of transient progenitors, as a wave of BMP signalling sweeps from anterior to posterior through HypFP cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings, contrasting the tuberal hypothalamus with other CNS regions.

claims.claim: Tuberal progenitor markers are first detected co-incident with pSMAD1/5/8 in aHypFP cells.
claims.source: First, tuberal progenitor markers are first detected co-incident with pSMAD1/5/8 in aHypFP cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial and temporal analysis of marker expression shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: As tuberal progenitors are generated, and the tuberal hypothalamus lengthens, pSMAD1/5/8 consistently straddles the border of aHypFP and posterior-most tuberal progenitor cells.
claims.source: As tuberal progenitors are generated, and the tuberal hypothalamus lengthens, pSMAD1/5/8 consistently straddles the border of aHypFP and posterior-most tuberal progenitor cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the spatial analysis of pSMAD1/5/8 expression over developmental time shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Ectopic BMP signalling can induce tuberal hypothalamic progenitors from HypFP cells that normally fate-map to the posterior (mammillary) hypothalamus.
claims.source: Second, gain-of-function studies demonstrate that ectopic BMP signalling can induce tuberal hypothalamic progenitors from HypFP cells that normally fate-map to the posterior (mammillary) hypothalamus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments with BMP2/7 treatment of posterior explants shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The ability of aHypFP cells to give rise to tuberal progenitors can be almost completely prevented by exposure to the BMP inhibitor, Noggin.
claims.source: Conversely, the ability of aHypFP cells to give rise to tuberal progenitors can be almost completely prevented by exposure to the BMP inhibitor, Noggin.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture experiments with Noggin treatment shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Fate-mapping studies at HH10 demonstrate the spatial relationship between HypFP cells and tuberal progenitors: anterior-most tuberal progenitors are generated from aHypFP cells, with more posterior tuberal progenitors generated from more posterior HypFP cells.
claims.source: Finally, fate-mapping studies at HH10 demonstrate the spatial relationship between HypFP cells and tuberal progenitors: anterior-most tuberal progenitors are generated from aHypFP cells, with more posterior tuberal progenitors generated from more posterior HypFP cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fate-mapping experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: A steady stream of tuberal progenitors is laid down in the wake of a travelling active BMP zone, that passes from anterior to posterior through HypFP cells.
claims.source: Our fate-mapping studies support the idea that a steady stream of tuberal progenitors is laid down in the wake of a travelling active BMP zone, that passes from anterior to posterior through HypFP cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the fate-mapping and pSMAD1/5/8 expression data.

claims.claim: Most, if not all, tuberal SIX6+ve anterior cells transiently activate BMP Smads and express TBX2, and are derived from FOXA2-expressing HypFP cells.
claims.source: While we cannot exclude that there may be tuberal progenitors that have a different history, and do not require BMP signalling (see below), our results indicate that most, if not all, tuberal SIX6+ve anterior cells transiently activate BMP Smads and express TBX2, and are derived from FOXA2-expressing HypFP cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings, with a caveat about possible alternative pathways.

claims.claim: As tuberal progenitors are generated, the anterior region expands dramatically, resulting in the rapid separation of the telencephalon and the floor plate.
claims.source: Building on our previous studies (Fu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2022), we show, moreover, that as tuberal progenitors are generated, the anterior region expands dramatically, resulting in the rapid separation of the telencephalon and the floor plate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of marker expression over time, combined with citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The wave of BMP signalling could provide a mechanism for temporal patterning of tuberal neurogenic progenitors, with the time at which HypFP cells are exposed to BMPs determining their future identity.
claims.source: The wave of BMP signalling could provide a mechanism for temporal patterning of tuberal neurogenic progenitors, with the time at which HypFP cells are exposed to BMPs determining their future identity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, proposing a mechanism for how BMP signaling could pattern the tuberal hypothalamus.

claims.claim: The upregulation of SOXE, ID and ONECUT family transcription factors, as well as differential expression of the SHH, WNT, FGF and NOTCH pathway components, could potentially determine the specification of distinct tuberal neuronal and glial subtypes as they encounter BMP signalling.
claims.source: The upregulation of SOXE, ID and ONECUT family transcription factors, as well as differential expression of the SHH, WNT, FGF and NOTCH pathway components, could potentially determine the specification of distinct tuberal neuronal and glial subtypes as they encounter BMP signalling.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the scRNA-Seq data, proposing candidate regulators of cell fate specification.

claims.claim: Many previous studies point to the importance of SHH in tuberal neurogenesis.
claims.source: Many previous studies point to the importance of SHH in tuberal neurogenesis (Carreno et al., 2017; Corman et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2017; Shimogori et al., 2010; Szabó et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: SHH and BMP signals/signalling often act antagonistically in neural tube patterning.
claims.source: This, and the fact that SHH and BMP signals/signalling often act antagonistically in neural tube patterning (Ulloa and Briscoe, 2007) are counter-intuitive to our finding that BMP signalling is critical to tuberal development.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature on neural tube patterning.

claims.claim: BMP plays a role in the initial specification of tuberal progenitors by inhibiting FST.
claims.source: First, one possibility is that BMP plays a role in the initial specification of tuberal progenitors by inhibiting FST. Here, we report that BMPs can suppress FST expression, and previously we have shown that FST inhibits hypothalamic induction (Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observation that BMPs suppress FST, combined with citation to previous work showing FST inhibits hypothalamic induction.

claims.claim: BMPs can suppress FST expression.
claims.source: Here, we report that BMPs can suppress FST expression, and previously we have shown that FST inhibits hypothalamic induction (Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that FST expression is eliminated after BMP bead implantation.

claims.claim: FST inhibits hypothalamic induction.
claims.source: Here, we report that BMPs can suppress FST expression, and previously we have shown that FST inhibits hypothalamic induction (Kim et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: BMP signalling is needed only for the initial specification of TBX2+ve posterior tuberal progenitors and must be switched off for these to progress to the anterior tuberal programme.
claims.source: Second, our experiments make it clear that BMP signalling is needed only for the initial specification of TBX2+ve posterior tuberal progenitors (Manning et al., 2006) and must be switched off for these to progress to the anterior tuberal programme: BMP inhibition in HH15 explants led to the loss of posterior, and the gain of anterior tuberal markers; conversely, prolonged exposure of nascent tuberal progenitors to BMPs at HH10 compromised anterior tuberal development.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo experiments with Noggin treatment at different time points and BMP bead implantation experiments, combined with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: By ensuring the sustained generation of appropriate numbers of SIX6/SHH progenitors, BMP signalling supports the development of a continued source of SHH-producing cells that sustain the tuberal neurogenic programme.
claims.source: We suggest that by ensuring the sustained generation of appropriate numbers of SIX6/SHH progenitors, BMP signalling supports the development of a continued source of SHH-producing cells that sustain the tuberal neurogenic programme.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observations that BMP is needed for posterior progenitor specification and that loss of anterior progenitors correlates with loss of posterior progenitors.

claims.claim: Without the continued specification of posterior tuberal progenitors, a smaller SIX6/SHH+ve anterior tuberal domain may be inadequate to support the tuberal programme.
claims.source: Without the continued specification of posterior tuberal progenitors, a smaller SIX6/SHH+ve anterior tuberal domain may be inadequate to support the tuberal programme (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, proposing a mechanism for the interdependence of anterior and posterior domains.

claims.claim: While posterior tuberal progenitors give rise to anterior tuberal progenitors, anterior progenitors generate signals that maintain posterior progenitors.
claims.source: Intriguingly, while posterior tuberal progenitors give rise to anterior tuberal progenitors, our results support previous observations that anterior progenitors generate signals that maintain posterior progenitors: the loss or reduction of SHH+ve anterior progenitors (in response to excessive BMP signalling) correlates, at HH18, with a loss or reduction of posterior tuberal progenitors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that loss of anterior progenitors after BMP treatment correlates with loss of posterior progenitors.

claims.claim: A transient reduction in SHH signalling disrupts FGF10+ve posterior progenitors in chick.
claims.source: Chick studies have previously shown that a transient reduction in SHH signalling disrupts FGF10+ve posterior progenitors (Fu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: As in the developing cerebellum, SHH from more differentiated cells promotes proliferation of earlier-stage progenitors in the tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.source: We therefore propose that, as in the developing cerebellum, SHH from more differentiated cells promotes proliferation of earlier-stage progenitors (Lewis et al., 2004; Wechsler-Reya and Scott, 1999; Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on analogy to the cerebellum, supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The loss/reduction of tuberal markers following prolonged BMP exposure is accompanied by a significant decrease in proliferating cells.
claims.source: Supporting this, the loss/reduction of tuberal markers seen following prolonged BMP exposure is accompanied by a significant decrease in proliferating cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of pH3+ cells in BMP-treated embryos shown in Figure 6Z.

claims.claim: Despite the loss of tuberal progenitors in BMP-exposed embryos, neurogenic (DLL1/ASCL1) and tuberal neuronal markers (ISL1/NR5A1/POMC) were detected.
claims.source: Finally, despite the loss of tuberal progenitors in BMP-exposed embryos, neurogenic (DLL1/ASCL1) and tuberal neuronal markers (ISL1/NR5A1/POMC) were detected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by marker expression analysis in BMP-treated embryos.

claims.claim: The presence of neurogenic and neuronal markers in BMP-exposed embryos is associated with a reduction in HES5, suggesting that Notch signalling is compromised.
claims.source: This was furthermore associated with a reduction in HES5, suggesting that Notch signalling is also compromised in these embryos.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of HES5 expression in BMP-treated embryos, combined with inference about Notch signaling.

claims.claim: Reduced Notch signalling would be expected to result in premature neuronal differentiation of hypothalamic neurons.
claims.source: This would be expected to result in premature neuronal differentiation of hypothalamic neurons (Aujla et al., 2013; Place et al., 2022; Ratié et al., 2013), providing a possible explanation for the presence of these markers even as progenitor development is heavily compromised.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Notch signaling in hypothalamic development, combined with inference.

claims.claim: The delicate balance of FST, BMP, SHH, FGF and Notch signalling ensures the correct balance between progenitor specification, proliferation and neurogenesis in the tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.source: Our results overall suggest that the delicate balance of FST, BMP, SHH, FGF and Notch signalling ensures the correct balance between progenitor specification, proliferation and neurogenesis, laying the groundwork for the further development of this highly complex hypothalamic region (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings, proposing an integrated model of signaling interactions.

claims.claim: Tuberal patterning is largely complete by HH14.
claims.source: Our ex vivo studies show that tuberal patterning is largely complete by HH14.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo experiments with Noggin treatment at different time points shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: By HH20/21, posterior tuberal progenitor cells undergo a significant change, upregulating VIM and FABP7, markers of radial glial cells.
claims.source: Our in silico bioinformatic analysis indicates that by HH20/21, posterior tuberal progenitor cells undergo a significant change, upregulating VIM and FABP7, markers of radial glial cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Elsewhere in the CNS, the transition of neuroepithelial cells to radial glial cells coincides with the onset of stem-like character.
claims.source: Elsewhere in the CNS, the transition of neuroepithelial cells to radial glial cells coincides with the onset of stem-like character, and potentially, this is true also in the posterior tuberal hypothalamus.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about CNS development, with speculation about its applicability to the tuberal hypothalamus.

claims.claim: In all vertebrates examined to date, specialised radial glial-like cells, termed tanycytes, form the critical constituents of a stem cell-like niche that is present in the adult hypothalamus, situated in the median eminence, adjacent to the pituitary gland.

results.result: The tuberal hypothalamus is progressively generated from hypothalamic floor plate-like (HypFP) cells through a conveyor-belt mechanism. A wave of BMP signaling (marked by pSMAD1/5/8) sweeps from anterior to posterior through HypFP cells, generating tuberal progenitors sequentially. Fate-mapping studies demonstrate that anterior-most tuberal progenitors derive from anterior HypFP cells, while more posterior tuberal progenitors derive from more posterior HypFP cells. As progenitors become distanced from BMP signals, they lose pSMAD1/5/8, downregulate posterior markers (TBX2), and upregulate anterior markers (SIX6, SHH) and neurogenic markers (ASCL1, ISL1).
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C66 are strongly supported by comprehensive fate-mapping experiments (C55-C61), spatial-temporal marker expression analysis (C38-C54), and pSMAD1/5/8 immunolabeling (C48-C54). The conveyor-belt model (C62) is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including DiI/DiO fate-mapping showing cells maintain relative positions (C61), and the observation that pSMAD1/5/8+ cells at HH10 give rise to anterior progenitors at HH17 (C55-C58). The sequential generation model (C66) is supported by the spatial progression of markers and the temporal dynamics of BMP signaling.

results.result: From HH10 onwards, hypothalamic neuroepithelium-intrinsic factors are sufficient to maintain tuberal hypothalamic regionalization and neurogenesis. BMP2 and BMP7 are expressed both in Rathke's pouch/ectoderm and in hypothalamic neuroepithelial cells. Ex vivo culture experiments demonstrate that isolated HH10 hypothalamic explants, cultured in the absence of surrounding tissues, develop organized tuberal domains (SIX6, TBX2, SHH, FGF10) by HH13 equivalent and generate spatial patterns similar to in vivo (ISL1/SHH, pSMAD1/5/8, EMX2 domains) by HH24 equivalent.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 are well-supported by ex vivo explant culture experiments (C72-C74) showing that isolated hypothalamic tissue develops appropriate marker expression and spatial organization without extrinsic signals. The expression of BMP2/7 in hypothalamic cells (C68-C69) is documented by HCR in situ hybridization. However, the claim about early requirement for extrinsic BMPs (C71) relies on citations to prior work rather than data presented here. The explant experiments provide strong evidence for neuroepithelial-intrinsic maintenance from HH10 onward.

results.result: BMP signaling initiates tuberal progenitor specification but must be eliminated for progression to anterior neurogenic progenitors. Gain-of-function experiments show that BMP2/7 treatment of posterior (HH6-8) explants induces tuberal markers (TBX2, SIX6, NR5A1, POMC). Loss-of-function experiments with Noggin demonstrate that BMP inhibition from the outset prevents tuberal marker expression, while delayed Noggin treatment (after HH10) allows anterior specification but prevents posterior progenitor generation. Specification of both anterior and posterior progenitors is complete by HH14.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C93 are strongly supported by systematic gain- and loss-of-function experiments both in vivo and ex vivo. The BMP2/7 treatment experiments (C76-C79) clearly demonstrate sufficiency for inducing tuberal fate. The temporal Noggin experiments (C85-C93) provide strong evidence for the biphasic requirement: BMP needed initially but must be removed for anterior progression. The conclusion that specification is complete by HH14 (C93, C127) is well-supported by the observation that Noggin treatment after HH14 has minimal effect. Statistical significance is reported for key findings (C81).

results.result: Excessive BMP exposure disrupts tuberal progenitor tissue homeostasis. Ectopic BMP2/7 beads implanted at HH10 acutely reduce/eliminate SIX6/SHH+ anterior tuberal progenitors and maintain cells in an early 'mixed' state (SIX6/TBX2/SHH+) at HH13. By HH18, prolonged BMP exposure leads to loss of both anterior and posterior tuberal progenitors, accompanied by reduced proliferation (pH3+ cells), decreased HES5 expression, and morphological abnormalities including failure of optic stalk narrowing.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C116 are well-supported by in vivo BMP2/7 bead implantation experiments analyzed at multiple time points (HH13 and HH18) using extensive multiplex HCR. The acute effects on anterior progenitors (C94-C100) and delayed effects on posterior progenitors (C101-C102) are documented with quantification showing statistical significance (C96: p<0.05; C101: n=4 reduced, n=2 eliminated). The reduction in proliferation (C114) is quantified with statistical significance. The interpretation regarding Notch signaling (C110-C112) is supported by HES5 expression data, though the lack of change in DLL1/ELAVL4 (C112) suggests complexity that is appropriately acknowledged (C113).

results.result: Posterior tuberal progenitors undergo temporal changes in transcriptional profile. scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells (which overlap with pSMAD1/5/8+ cells) reveals differential gene expression between early (HH8-10) and late (HH15-21) stages. Early progenitors show enriched expression of BMP2/7, CHRD, SST, and SHISA2, while later progenitors upregulate CRABP1, WNT5A, CTGF, CTNNB1, NOTCH pathway components (LFNG, HES5), and transcription factors (ONECUT1, ID1/2/4, SOX8/9). By HH20/21, radial glial markers VIM and FABP7 are upregulated, suggesting transition toward tanycyte fate. Ex vivo experiments show that after HH15, BMPs actively repress the anterior tuberal program.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C135 are supported by scRNA-Seq analysis of FGF10+ cells across developmental stages (C118-C126) with validation by HCR for ID2/ID4 (C125). The temporal switch in BMP response (C128-C130) is supported by ex vivo experiments showing Noggin treatment at HH15 eliminates TBX2 and promotes anterior markers. The upregulation of radial glial markers (C134) is documented in the scRNA-Seq data. However, the interpretation that these changes reflect transition to tanycytes (C135, C169) is speculative and relies on inference combined with citations to prior work. The claim would be strengthened by direct lineage tracing or functional validation of the proposed gliogenic program.

results.result: As later-specified posterior tuberal progenitors are generated, early-specified anterior tuberal progenitors become progressively more distant from BMP signals and differentiate into tuberal neurogenic cells. This results in rapid expansion of the anterior region and separation of telencephalon and floor plate.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C31-C32, and C145 are supported by spatial analysis of marker expression over time showing progressive anterior displacement of early-specified cells and expansion of the SIX6/SHH domain. The fate-mapping data (C55-C61) demonstrate that cells maintain relative positions while the tissue expands anteriorly. The separation of telencephalon and floor plate is documented in the marker expression data (C34, C145). However, the claim that cells 'differentiate into tuberal neurogenic cells' (C4) could be more precisely stated as 'progress to neurogenic progenitors' based on the marker data showing ASCL1 and ISL1 expression.

results.result: A delicate balance of FST, BMP, SHH, FGF, and Notch signaling ensures correct balance between progenitor specification, proliferation, and neurogenesis. BMP may initially specify tuberal progenitors by inhibiting FST. BMP is needed only for initial specification of TBX2+ posterior progenitors and must be switched off for progression to anterior program. SHH from anterior progenitors may promote proliferation of posterior progenitors, creating interdependence between domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C163 represent an integrated model of signaling interactions, but several key components are speculative or incompletely supported. The FST suppression by BMP (C151) is documented, but the mechanistic role in tuberal specification (C150) is inferred. The requirement for BMP in initial specification (C153) is well-supported, but the proposed mechanism whereby BMP supports sustained SHH production (C154-C155) is speculative. The feedback from anterior to posterior progenitors (C156) is inferred from correlation (loss of anterior correlates with loss of posterior) rather than direct demonstration of causality. The proposed SHH-mediated proliferation mechanism (C158) is based on analogy to cerebellum rather than direct evidence in this system. These claims would benefit from additional functional experiments to test the proposed signaling interactions.

results.result: The molecular changes in later posterior tuberal progenitors may reflect onset of transition from neurogenic FGF10+ neuroepithelial cells to FGF10+ radial glial-like tanycytes. The upregulation of SOX8/9 and ID genes may be linked to neuroepithelial-to-radial glial transition, as SOX9 regulates this transition in spinal cord. This work identifies candidate regulators governing development of the adult hypothalamic stem cell niche.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C170 are largely speculative interpretations of the molecular data. While the upregulation of SOX8/9, ID genes, VIM, and FABP7 is documented (C124, C134), the interpretation that this reflects gliogenic transition (C132, C135) is based on analogy to other systems (C131, C133) rather than direct functional evidence. The connection to adult tanycytes (C135, C169) relies on FGF10 expression as a common marker and citations to prior work, but lacks lineage tracing or functional validation. The claim about stem cell niche development (C170) is a reasonable inference but remains to be tested. These claims represent interesting hypotheses that require additional experimental validation, including lineage tracing from FGF10+ progenitors to adult tanycytes and functional testing of candidate regulators.

results.result: Background claims establishing the importance of the tuberal hypothalamus, its evolutionary conservation, cellular composition (neurons and tanycytes), and prior knowledge about its development including the existence of anterior and posterior domains, the role of various signaling pathways, and conservation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C29, C136, C148-C149 are background/context claims supported by citations to established literature. These provide the scientific foundation and rationale for the current study. The claims accurately represent prior knowledge in the field based on the citations provided. These are not novel findings of the current manuscript but rather establish the context and gaps in knowledge that motivate the present work.

results.result: In the tuberal hypothalamus, spatial pattern emerges through transient progenitors as a wave of BMP signaling sweeps anterior to posterior, contrasting with other CNS regions where temporal switches in stem-like progenitors generate waves of precursors. The wave of BMP signaling could provide a mechanism for temporal patterning, with timing of BMP exposure determining cell identity. Differential expression of transcription factors and signaling components could determine specification of distinct subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C137, C146-C147 represent the conceptual framework and mechanistic interpretation of the findings. C137 is well-supported by the data showing sequential generation through transient progenitors (C2-C66) and contrasts this with established mechanisms in other CNS regions (C136). However, C146-C147 are more speculative, proposing mechanisms for how BMP timing and transcriptional changes could determine cell fate. While these are reasonable interpretations of the data, they represent hypotheses that would require additional functional experiments (e.g., timed BMP exposure experiments, perturbation of candidate transcription factors) to definitively establish causality. The claims appropriately use conditional language ('could provide', 'could potentially determine').

results.result: Tuberal patterning is largely complete by HH14.
results.evaluation: Claim C164 is supported by ex vivo experiments showing that Noggin treatment after HH14 has minimal effect on marker expression (C92-C93), indicating that specification decisions have been made by this stage. This is a clear, well-supported conclusion from the temporal Noggin experiments.
